newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia rate cut not expected, not ruled out.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia rate cut not expected, not ruled out.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia board meets for the first time in 1997 today and while analysts generally don't expect a rate move this month all eyes will be on trading screens at 9.30 a.m. each day just in case.
The RBA cut interest rates three times in the second half of 1996, with the first in July and third in December catching the markets largely off guard.
The median forecast of 30 economists surveyed by Reuters put the chance of a rate cut in February at 40 percent, despite news last week of a continuing moderation in inflation.
However, the median expectation rises to an even money bet after February as economists believe the RBA will wait on the outcome of an important union wage case before making any move.

By then the RBA will also have some feeling of how the economy started 1997 and may be able to see the impact of the last two rate cuts delivered in November and December, before deciding whether another rate cut was justified.

"We think that they'll probably want to see the activity indicators through the course of the early months of 1997, and I think more importantly they'll want to see wages information -- not only the wages data this Thursday, but also any new from the 'living wage' claim," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
The 'living wage' claim, lodged by the Australian Council of Trade Unions, is currently under consideration by the Industrial Relations Commission with a result expected by early March.
The claim proposes that all workers not covered by workplace agreements receive an 8.75 percent increase in award wages and and three A$20 a week safety net adjustments over three years.

In its December Bulletin, the RBA warned that, based on its calculations, "the full living wage claim would imply a marked acceleration of wages growth," putting that accleration at close to two percentage points.
This would take aggregate growth to well over five percent, the RBA said. Wages growth above five percent is seen by economists as being above the RBA's "comfort zone" on wages.

Despite this there is still a chance the RBA could cut rates before the outcome the wage case is known, especially if the economy continues to perform on the low side of expectations, and favourable wages data for the three months to November is received on Thursday.
Median forecasts centre on a 0.9 percent rise in the quarter to be 3.6 percent higher over the year, which would be a moderation in quarterly and annual terms from August levels.
Schroders Australia chief economist Brett Allender said that while the RBA would probably not ease in February, such a move was not out the question.
"The fact of the matter is that they did ease twice in two months at the end of 1996, and I think that gives some insight into their feelings where the economy was headed," he said.

Economsts said the recent fall in the Australian dollar, from above US$0.80 when it was cited as a supporting factor behind the December cut to a low of just under US$0.76 last week, would not rule out another cut, especially as it had held up better in trade weighted terms.
"The RBA is likely to view the Australian dollar's recent softness as posing little risk to its inflation objectives," ANZ Treasury economists said.

Keeping the markets nervous each day is the fact that, unlike its U.S. counterpart, the RBA can change rates on any day it likes, as was the case in December when the cut came over a week after the RBA's last board meeting.
Any change in policy is made at 9.30 a.m. (2230 GMT), when the RBA announces its monetary operations for the day.
The RBA's current overnight cash rate is 6.0 percent.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
